blocks.text: A 17-year-old tells the triage nurse she took 'a few painkillers' last night after an argument and feels fine. Feeling fine is exactly how a paracetamol overdose looks in the first day, which is why poisoned patients are managed on risk, not on how they look.

blocks.markdown: In the emergency department most poisoned patients are managed with **supportive care** rather than specific antidotes. Structure the approach as: resuscitate with ABCDE; assess the **risk** (what agent, how much, when, by what route, with what co-ingestants, whether intentional); decide whether any **decontamination** or **antidote** is indicated; monitor; and carry out a **psychosocial and suicide risk assessment** before discharge. In the UK, TOXBASE and the National Poisons Information Service (NPIS) provide agent-specific advice; always check current local sources.

blocks.title: Antidote
blocks.text: A drug that specifically counteracts the effect of a poison, either by reversing receptor action (naloxone, flumazenil) or by neutralising a toxic metabolite (acetylcysteine). Antidotes have their own risks and are used for defined indications, not as a routine.

items: Resuscitate: protect the airway, support breathing, treat shock, check capillary glucose and take an ECG (many drugs prolong QRS or QT).
Take a history from the patient, family, ambulance crew and packaging: agent, dose (estimate the maximum possible), time, route, co-ingestants, alcohol.
Examine for a toxidrome: a pattern of signs that suggests a drug class.
Send targeted tests: paracetamol level (timed after ingestion), salicylate, U&E, glucose, blood gas, as advised by TOXBASE.
Consider decontamination, then antidote or enhanced elimination as indicated.
Observe for the required period and complete a mental health assessment.

blocks.markdown: **Decontamination** has narrow indications. Activated charcoal binds many drugs in the gut and, as generally taught, is considered for a potentially serious ingestion of a charcoal-binding drug within about an hour, provided the airway is safe or protected. Induced vomiting and gastric lavage are not routine because of aspiration and little benefit. Always check current TOXBASE advice.

rows: Paracetamol
Often asymptomatic early; later nausea, right upper quadrant pain, raised ALT, liver failure
N-acetylcysteine (replenishes glutathione, neutralises the toxic metabolite NAPQI)
Use the timed level and national guidance to decide; repeat or staggered ingestions are higher risk
Opioids
Reduced consciousness, slow shallow breathing, pinpoint pupils
Naloxone (opioid receptor antagonist), titrated to breathing
Short duration of action, so re-sedation can occur; may precipitate withdrawal
Benzodiazepines
Drowsiness, reduced reflexes, usually mild respiratory depression alone
Supportive care; flumazenil only in selected cases
Flumazenil can provoke seizures in dependent patients or mixed overdoses, so it is not routine
blocks.caption: Selected antidotes; doses, nomograms and treatment thresholds must be checked against current TOXBASE, NICE and local guidance

blocks.title: Estimating a paracetamol ingestion
blocks.prompt: A 70 kg adult reports taking 28 tablets of 500 mg paracetamol. Calculate the dose in mg/kg and explain how it is used.

steps.text: Dose per kilogram = 14,000 mg / 70 kg = 200 mg/kg.

This estimate is the maximum possible exposure, since the patient may have taken less. It is a risk screen, not a treatment decision: treatment is decided by the time since ingestion, a timed serum level (not taken before 4 hours) and current national guidance.
Because paracetamol toxicity can develop silently, arrange appropriate testing and, where indicated, start N-acetylcysteine as directed by TOXBASE, then assess ALT and INR.

blocks.answer: 200 mg/kg; a high-risk exposure by dose, to be acted on with a timed level and local guidance.

blocks.markdown: **Environmental injury.** *Hypothermia* is a core temperature below 35 C. It slows metabolism, causes confusion and loss of shivering at lower temperatures, bradycardia and arrhythmias; the cold myocardium is irritable, so rough handling can precipitate ventricular fibrillation. Management is gentle handling, a core temperature measurement (low-reading thermometer), removal of wet clothing, insulation and rewarming, active in moderate to severe cases. Resuscitation attempts may need to be prolonged in severe hypothermia. *Heat illness* spans heat exhaustion (sweating, weakness, normal mental state) to **heat stroke**: a core temperature of about 40 C or higher with central nervous system dysfunction (confusion, seizures, coma). Heat stroke is a medical emergency needing rapid external cooling with ABCDE support. *Drowning* is respiratory impairment from submersion; the dominant problem is **hypoxia**, so airway and ventilation come first, with rescue breaths prioritised in cardiac arrest from drowning (check current RCUK guidance).

rows: Hypothermia
Cold, confused, shivering stops at low temperatures, bradycardia, arrhythmia
Gentle handling, insulate, rewarm, monitor ECG
Heat exhaustion
Sweating, headache, nausea, tachycardia, mentation intact
Move to cool place, oral or IV fluids, rest
Heat stroke
Core temperature about 40 C or more, altered mental state, hot skin
Rapid cooling, ABCDE, treat complications
Drowning
Hypoxia, cough, respiratory distress, reduced consciousness
Airway, ventilation, oxygen, treat hypothermia
blocks.caption: Environmental emergencies

blocks.title: Rewarming rate
blocks.prompt: A patient's core temperature is 31.0 C on arrival and 33.5 C five hours later during active rewarming. Calculate the average rewarming rate and comment.

steps.text: Rate = rise / time = 2.5 / 5 = 0.5 C per hour.
Comment: continue core temperature monitoring and ECG, because rewarming can unmask hypovolaemia and arrhythmia; target rates and methods follow the current local or national hypothermia protocol.

blocks.answer: 0.5 C per hour (verify target rates against the local protocol).

blocks.title: Do not rely on how well the patient looks
blocks.text: Paracetamol, some sustained-release preparations and some other toxins cause delayed harm. A well-looking patient may need antidote treatment, and a flat-looking one may be saved by supportive care alone.

points: Poisoned patients are managed by ABCDE, risk assessment, targeted tests and mostly supportive care, using TOXBASE or NPIS advice.
Key antidotes: acetylcysteine for paracetamol, naloxone for opioids (short-acting, re-sedation possible), flumazenil only selectively for benzodiazepines.
Hypothermia needs gentle handling and rewarming; heat stroke needs rapid cooling; drowning is a problem of hypoxia.
Check all doses, nomograms and thresholds against current guidance.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old is brought in drowsy after a suspected intentional overdose of unknown tablets taken some hours earlier. Describe your approach, including resuscitation, risk assessment, investigations, the role of decontamination and what must be done before discharge.
markingGuide: Starts with ABCDE, protecting the airway and supporting breathing and circulation, and checks capillary glucose.
Takes history of agent, dose, time, route, co-ingestants and intent from patient, relatives, ambulance crew and packaging.
Looks for a toxidrome and obtains an ECG.
Sends targeted tests such as timed paracetamol level, salicylate, U&E, blood gas.
Consults TOXBASE or the National Poisons Information Service.
Considers activated charcoal only for suitable ingestions within a short window with a protected airway; no routine vomiting or lavage.
Observes appropriately, completes a mental health and suicide risk assessment and involves psychiatry before discharge.
questions.explanation: Most overdoses are managed by supportive care and risk-based decisions. The psychosocial assessment is part of the emergency management because the poisoning is often intentional.

questions.stem: A conscious, protected-airway adult presents 40 minutes after ingesting a potentially serious dose of a drug that binds to charcoal. Which statement about gut decontamination is most consistent with generally taught practice?

options.text: Activated charcoal may be considered, following current TOXBASE advice
Induced vomiting with syrup of ipecac is the preferred method
Routine gastric lavage should be performed for every overdose
No decontamination is ever considered

questions.correctOptionText: Activated charcoal may be considered, following current TOXBASE advice

distractorRationale.a: Correct: charcoal is an option within a short time window for suitable drugs when the airway is safe.
distractorRationale.b: Induced vomiting is not recommended because of aspiration risk and poor benefit.
distractorRationale.c: Lavage is not routine and carries risk.
distractorRationale.d: Decontamination has narrow but real indications.

questions.explanation: Decontamination is limited to specific scenarios: a potentially serious ingestion of a charcoal-binding agent within about an hour and a protected airway. Always check agent-specific advice and the local policy.

questions.stem: What is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning, and what is its principal mechanism?

options.text: N-acetylcysteine, which replenishes glutathione and detoxifies the toxic metabolite NAPQI
Naloxone, which blocks opioid receptors
Flumazenil, which blocks GABA-A benzodiazepine sites
Vitamin K, which restores clotting factors

questions.correctOptionText: N-acetylcysteine, which replenishes glutathione and detoxifies the toxic metabolite NAPQI

distractorRationale.d: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not paracetamol.

questions.explanation: In overdose, normal conjugation pathways saturate and more paracetamol is converted to NAPQI, which depletes glutathione and injures hepatocytes. N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione and reduces liver injury, and is most effective when started early; decisions follow the timed level and current national guidance.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old is found collapsed with a respiratory rate of 6 per minute, pinpoint pupils and needle marks. Naloxone is given and he wakes up and breathes well. Which warning is most important?

options.text: Naloxone may wear off before the opioid, so re-sedation and respiratory depression can recur and he needs monitoring
Naloxone has a longer duration than most opioids so no observation is required
Naloxone should be withheld from patients who are breathing slowly
He can be discharged immediately because he is awake

questions.correctOptionText: Naloxone may wear off before the opioid, so re-sedation and respiratory depression can recur and he needs monitoring

distractorRationale.a: Correct: naloxone's duration is often shorter than that of the opioid, so recurrence is possible.
distractorRationale.b: Naloxone's effect is generally shorter than that of many opioids.
distractorRationale.c: Naloxone is indicated precisely for respiratory depression.

questions.explanation: Naloxone competitively blocks opioid receptors, but the effect lasts a shorter time than many opioids, especially long-acting ones. A period of observation, and sometimes an infusion, is required; follow current guidance.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old has taken an overdose of diazepam alone. He has GCS 11, normal oxygen saturation and a respiratory rate of 14. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Supportive care with airway monitoring; flumazenil is not routinely given
Immediate large-dose flumazenil for every benzodiazepine overdose
Induced vomiting
Intravenous N-acetylcysteine

questions.correctOptionText: Supportive care with airway monitoring; flumazenil is not routinely given

distractorRationale.a: Correct: isolated benzodiazepine overdose usually does well with supportive care.
distractorRationale.b: Flumazenil can provoke seizures, especially in dependent patients or mixed overdoses, so it is not routine.
distractorRationale.c: Inducing vomiting risks aspiration in a drowsy patient.

questions.explanation: Benzodiazepine overdose alone seldom causes life-threatening respiratory depression, so supportive care is usually enough. Flumazenil is reserved for selected cases because of the seizure risk, and a mixed overdose must be considered.

questions.stem: A 80 kg adult reports taking 36 tablets of 500 mg paracetamol. Calculate the maximum reported dose in mg/kg. Give your answer in mg/kg.
questions.explanation: Total dose = 36 x 500 mg = 18,000 mg. Dividing by body weight, 18,000 / 80 = 225 mg/kg. This is used to estimate risk, with timing and a paracetamol level guiding treatment according to current guidance.

questions.stem: A hillwalker is brought in with a core temperature of 29 C, bradycardia and reduced consciousness. Which principle of care is most appropriate?

options.text: Handle gently with ECG monitoring and begin rewarming, since the cold heart is prone to ventricular fibrillation
Rub the limbs vigorously to restore circulation
Give rapid warm fluids and move him briskly to the ward
Give repeated high-dose adrenaline immediately

questions.correctOptionText: Handle gently with ECG monitoring and begin rewarming, since the cold heart is prone to ventricular fibrillation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: gentle handling reduces the risk of precipitating arrhythmia.
distractorRationale.b: Vigorous movement can precipitate VF and sends cold blood to the core.
distractorRationale.c: Brisk movement and rough handling are avoided.
distractorRationale.d: Drug use is limited in severe hypothermia and is not the first step.

questions.explanation: At low core temperatures the myocardium is irritable, and rough handling can trigger ventricular fibrillation. Care emphasises monitoring, insulation, rewarming and a core temperature measurement, following current hypothermia guidance.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old soldier collapses during a hot-weather march. He is confused, has hot skin and a core temperature of 41.5 C. What is the priority?

options.text: Rapid active cooling alongside ABCDE support
Antipyretics such as paracetamol alone
Oral fluids and rest
Warm blankets to prevent shivering

questions.correctOptionText: Rapid active cooling alongside ABCDE support

distractorRationale.a: Correct: heat stroke is treated with rapid external cooling and supportive care.
distractorRationale.b: Antipyretics are ineffective because the problem is not a raised hypothalamic set point.
distractorRationale.c: Oral fluids are insufficient for a confused patient with heat stroke.

questions.explanation: Confusion with a core temperature of about 40 C or more defines heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency where outcomes depend on how quickly the temperature is reduced. Cooling and organ support are given together.

questions.stem: During active rewarming a patient's core temperature rises from 30.4 C to 34.0 C over 6 hours. Calculate the average rewarming rate in degrees Celsius per hour.
questions.explanation: The rise is 34.0 - 30.4 = 3.6 C. Dividing by 6 hours gives 0.6 C per hour. Rewarming is monitored against the current local protocol.

questions.stem: Compare the presentation and emergency priorities of heat stroke, hypothermia and drowning.
markingGuide: Heat stroke: core temperature about 40 C or higher with CNS dysfunction (confusion, seizures); priority is rapid external cooling with ABCDE support.
Hypothermia: core temperature below 35 C, confusion, loss of shivering, bradycardia, arrhythmia; priority is gentle handling, monitoring, insulation and rewarming.
Drowning: hypoxia is the dominant problem; priority is airway and ventilation with oxygen, and rescue breaths in arrest.
States that drowning in cold water may coexist with hypothermia, which affects resuscitation duration.
Mentions that targets and protocols are checked against current guidance.
questions.explanation: Each condition has a different dominant physiological problem: heat, cold or hypoxia. Management targets that problem while maintaining ABCDE.
